notes.text: And fear came upon every soul — Of those who did not join with them: whereby persecution was prevented, till it was needful for them.

And sold their possessions — Their lands and houses; and goods - Their movables. And parted them to all as any one had need - To say the Christians did this only till the destruction of Jerusalem, is not true; for many did it long after. Not that there was any positive command for so doing: it needed not; for love constrained them. It was a natural fruit of that love wherewith each member of the community loved every other as his own soul. And if the whole Christian Church had continued in this spirit, this usage must have continued through all ages. To affirm therefore that Christ did not design it should continue, is neither more nor less than to affirm, that Christ did not design this measure of love should continue. I see no proof of this.

Continuing daily — breaking the bread - in the Lord's Supper, as did many Churches for some ages. They partook of their food with gladness and singleness of heart - They carried the same happy and holy temper through all their common actions: eating and working with the same spirit wherewith they prayed and received the Lord's Supper.
The Lord added daily such as were saved — From their sins: from the guilt and power of them.
Lie down — To repose myself at noon, as the manner was in those hot countries. Green - Where there is both delight and plenty of provisions.
Restoreth — Hebrew. He bringeth it back; from its errors and wandering. For - Not for any worth in me, but for the glory of his justice, and faithfulness, and goodness.
Thy rod and thy staff — Two words denoting the same thing, and both designing God's pastoral care over him.

A table — Thou furnishest me with plenty of provisions and comforts. Oil - With aromatic ointments, which were then used at great feasts; thy comforts delight my soul. Runneth over - Thou hast given me a plentiful portions, signified by the cup, given to the guests by the master of the feast. This psalm is generally thought to have been composed by David, upon bringing the ark of God from the house of Obed- edom, into the tabernacle which David had built for it, 2 Sam. vi, 12, 17. Wherein he hath a farther prospect to the temple, which he earnestly desired and intended to build. Moreover because the tabernacle, and temple, and ark, were types of Christ, and of his church and of heaven. David extended his thoughts to them also, or at least the Holy Ghost designed to comprehend them under these typical expressions. He shews God's sovereignty over the world, ver. 1, 2. Who shall receive his blessing, ver. 3-6. An exhortation to receive Christ, ver. 7-10. A psalm of David.

glossa.text: *A psalm of David.* ((CASS.)) The Prophet foretold the return of the people from Babylon. *The Lord ruleth me.* A psalm of mercy, enumerating ten graces, that all may hope in the mercy of God. ((AUG.)) The Church speaks of Christ.

*In a place of pasture.* ((CASS.)) The first grace, a place of pasture, that is, the divine word, which fattens those who meditate upon it. *Upon the water.* The second grace, the water of refreshment.

*My soul.* ((ID.)) The third grace, etc., *as far as* but first he brought me up upon the water of refreshment, first he converted my soul. *He hath led.* ((ID.)) The fourth, in that he led me upon the precepts of charity. *Upon the paths.* ((AUG.)) The narrower commandments and the more perfect counsels; as it were upon paths few just men walk, even as paths are narrower than roads.

*For though I shall walk.* ((CASS.)) The fifth, that in the shadow of death he fears no evils. *Thou art with me.* ((AUG.)) In the heart by faith, that after the shadow of death I may be with thee. *Thy rod.* ((CASS.)) The sixth, correction; or the rod is strictness, which converts vices. The staff is governance, which upholds the faithful.

*Thou hast prepared in my sight.* ((CASS.)) The seventh, the table of the Lord, the blessed banqueting, the fullness of faith, the heavenly food, of which the Apostle: *He that eateth and drinketh unworthily, eateth and drinketh judgment to himself. In my sight a table:* even if not that of the wicked. Of this it is said: *But these at the table of the rich man,* that is, of Christ, *know that thou too must prepare the like,* that is, to suffer as he did. *Thou hast anointed:* the eighth, the anointing of the head, namely of Christ, which was dried up by no barrenness of sin, whence the rest of the members rejoice, because from the head the ointment ran down upon the beard, the beard of Aaron, and unto the skirt of his garment. *And my chalice.* The ninth, the chalice, the blood of Christ, which so inebriates that it makes men sober. *Mine,* because I receive it. Or, thine, because thou givest it. The table and the chalice, flesh and blood, although they are one sacrament, yet under diverse species, because both are taken, are here set down separately.
*And mercy.* ((CASS.)) The tenth, mercy following after unto keeping, which goes before unto the conferring of grace.
*And that I may dwell.* ((HIER.)) This is joined to all the things above. As though: thou hast placed, thou hast brought up, thou hast led, etc., and this to the end that I may dwell.

notes.text: For conscience toward God — From a pure desire of pleasing him. Grief - Severe treatment.
Hereunto are ye — Christians. Called - To suffer wrongfully. Leaving you an example - When he went to God. That ye might follow his steps - Of innocence and patience.

In all these instances the example of Christ is peculiarly adapted to the state of servants, who easily slide either into sin or guile, reviling their fellowservants, or threatening them, the natural result of anger without power. He committed himself to him that judgeth righteously — The only solid ground of patience in affliction. Isaiah liii, 4, 6, 7, 9.

22, 23. In all these instances the example of Christ is peculiarly adapted to the state of servants, who easily slide either into sin or guile, reviling their fellowservants, or threatening them, the natural result of anger without power. He committed himself to him that judgeth righteously - The only solid ground of patience in affliction.

Who himself bore our sins — That is, the punishment due to them. In his afflicted, torn, dying body on the tree - The cross, whereon chiefly slaves or servants were wont to suffer. That we being dead to sin - Wholly delivered both from the guilt and power of it: indeed, without an atonement first made for the guilt, we could never have been delivered from the power. Might live to righteousness - Which is one only. The sins we had committed, and he bore, were manifold.
The bishop — The kind observer, inspector, or overseer of your souls.

glossa.text:
*If for conscience towards God.* If, for God who knows a good intention, some patient man is unjustly beaten by his lord, though he serve him well, and endures it, that is, accounts his sorrows light, this is grace, and by this he is made pleasing to God, and this the grace of faith requires.

*Suffering wrongfully.* If you suffer unjustly, you acquire the grace of God. For if you patiently bear the punishments inflicted by your masters, you, I say, sinning by refusing to obey them, and buffeted by those same masters, that is, often corrected by them, that through buffetings you may be led to obey, what grace will you have thereby? Nothing, on this account shall you receive from God.

*For unto this you are called.* He greatly glorifies the condition of servants, whom, well-doing and beaten without fault by cruel and wicked masters, he affirms to be imitators of the Lord's passion.

*Because Christ also. ((BEDA.))* Whereas above he instructed servants specially, now he instructs the whole Church, that he may recall to the memory of masters also what their author endured for their salvation or deliverance.

*But he delivered himself to him that judged him unjustly.* To those judging according to an unjust law, being himself just. Or, he delivered to God the Father those judging unjustly, that is, those who most wickedly condemned him, and pressed for his death, that by undergoing punishments they might be instructed. He touches upon the evangelical parable, where it is said that the good shepherd, leaving ninety-nine sheep in the desert, came to visit the one that had perished.

*And the bishop.* Or the visitor, which is the same thing. For a bishop, that is, an overseer, because *the eyes of the Lord are upon the just, and his ears unto their prayers.* And, *The Orient from on high hath visited us.*

notes.text: He that entereth not by the door — By Christ. He is the only lawful entrance. Into the sheepfold - The Church. He is a thief and a robber - In God's account. Such were all those teachers, to whom our Lord had just been speaking.

To him the door keeper openeth — Christ is considered as the shepherd, ver. 11. As the door in the first and following verses. And as it is not unworthy of Christ to be styled the door, by which both the sheep and the true pastor enter, so neither is it unworthy of God the Father to be styled the door keeper. See Acts xiv, 27; Colossians iv, 3; Rev. iii, 8; Acts xvi, 14. And the sheep hear his voice - The circumstances that follow, exactly agree with the customs of the ancient eastern shepherds. They called their sheep by name, went before them and the sheep followed them. So real Christians hear, listen to, understand, and obey the voice of the shepherd whom Christ hath sent. And he counteth them his own, dearer than any friend or brother: calleth, advises, directs each by name, and leadeth them out, in the paths of righteousness, beside the waters of comfort.

He goeth before them — In all the ways of God, teaching them in every point, by example as well as by precept; and the sheep follow him - They tread in his steps: for they know his voice - Having the witness in themselves that his words are the wisdom and the power of God. Reader, art thou a shepherd of souls? Then answer to God. Is it thus with thee and thy flock?

They will not follow a stranger — One whom Christ hath not sent, who doth not answer the preceding description. Him they will not follow - And who can constrain them to it? But will flee from him - As from the plague. For they know not the voice of strangers - They cannot relish it; it is harsh and grating to them. They find nothing of God therein.
They — The Pharisees, to whom our Lord more immediately spake, as appears from the close of the foregoing chapter.
I am the door — Christ is both the Door and the Shepherd, and all things.

Whosoever are come — Independently of me, assuming any part of my character, pretending, like your elders and rabbis, to a power over the consciences of men, attempting to make laws in the Church, and to teach their own traditions as the way of salvation: all those prophets and expounders of God's word, that enter not by the door of the sheepfold, but run before I have sent them by my Spirit. Our Lord seems in particular to speak of those that had undertaken this office since he began his ministry, are thieves -Stealing temporal profit to themselves, and robbers - Plundering and murdering the sheep.

If any one — As a sheep, enter in by me - Through faith, he shall be safe - From the wolf, and from those murdering shepherds. And shall go in and out - Shall continually attend on the shepherds whom I have sent; and shall find pasture - Food for his soul in all circumstances.
The thief cometh not but to steal, and to kill, and to destroy — That is, nothing else can be the consequence of a shepherd's coming, who does not enter in by me.

glossa.text: *Amen, amen I say to you.* Because the Pharisees boasted that they saw, which they would be able to do if they were Christ's sheep, the Lord sets forth against their arrogance a similitude of his flock, and of the door by which one enters into the sheepfold, showing that neither wisdom, nor the observance of the law, nor a good life avails anything except through him: without him they are nothing in whatever Jew, or Gentile and philosopher, or Pharisee who teach men to live blessedly, or heretic under the name of Christ; nor yet in Christ preaching, but all of them without him snatch away and kill. *By the door.* That is, through me, as he afterwards expounds. This gate is low: he who wishes to enter through it must humble himself, lest, if he stands upright, he strike against the low gate. *A thief.* Because he calls his own what belongs to another, that is, he makes God's sheep his own. A robber, because what he has stolen he kills. But all who hold and teach the truth in Christ the shepherd are one shepherd.

*Is the shepherd of the sheep.* Christ is properly the shepherd according to the office of feeding the sheep, as he himself afterwards expounds, who through himself as the door enters into the sheepfold of the sheep. But because others are sharers with him in the pastoral office, the things which are properly said of him are fitting to them also in their own manner. The door is that by which one enters; Christ therefore, the shepherd, is himself the door, and whoever is a shepherd under him enters through that same door into the hearts of the sheep; because if he preaches something else, the sheep do not hear; if Christ, the sheep of Christ acknowledge this voice.

*To him the porter openeth.* The porter, that is, Christ who opens himself, or Scripture which leads to Christ, or the Holy Spirit who teaches all truth.

*And the sheep,* etc. ((AUG.)) Some are true sheep, because the Lord knoweth, etc., *as far as* this no one who is his own despises, no stranger hears.

*But they understood not.* The predestined sheep for a time do not know themselves, nor do they hear the voice of the shepherd, but at the end they persevere; on the contrary the wolves for a time hear, but at the end they persevere.

*All,* etc. He is a thief who enters by simony or in some other way against Christ, and after he has entered kills by his bad example, and so is openly a robber. Nor is such a one to be called a hireling, therefore when the wolf comes he does not resist, but yields for a wage. If he does not resist the wolf tearing them by violence, he receives this wage, that he is not torn asunder along with the sheep; but afterwards, by living badly, he corrupts the sheep, and having now slipped back into the other party he becomes a thief or a robber, losing the name of hireling.

*If any man.* Here he plainly shows that not only the shepherd but the sheep also enter through the door. *And he shall go in.* Within, by thinking well; he shall go out, outwardly, by working well for the example of others. Or he shall go in into the Church, that here he may live by faith. Whence he says afterwards: *That they may have life.* And he shall go out of this life, that he may live for ever. Whence afterwards, and may have life more abundantly, and going in and going out shall find pastures.
*But to steal,* etc. He would steal, by usurping to himself what is another's; kill, by drawing them back from the faith; destroy, unto eternal damnation.

sermons.author: John Wesley

hymns.title: The Lord's my shepherd, I'll not want
The King of love my shepherd is
Come, let us eat, for now the feast is spread

praise.title: How Deep the Father's Love for Us

echoes.text: However there shall be no poor with you (for Yahweh will surely bless you in the land which Yahweh your God gives you for an inheritance to possess it) if only you diligently listen to Yahweh your God’s voice, to observe to do all this commandment which I command you this day.
echoes.note: The community 'had all things in common... and distributed to all, as any had need' (vv.44-45) realizes the Deuteronomic ideal that 'there shall be no poor among you' if Israel obeys, with goods shared so none lacks. Moderate volume via the 'need/no poor' motif; thematic coherence high, and Luke develops it again in Acts 4:34 ('there was not a needy person'), echoing Deut 15 directly, which supplies recurrence.

echoes.text: “‘You shall count from the next day after the Sabbath, from the day that you brought the sheaf of the wave offering; seven Sabbaths shall be completed: even to the next day after the seventh Sabbath you shall number fifty days; and you shall offer a new meal offering to Yahweh. You shall bring out of your habitations two loaves of bread for a wave offering made of two tenth parts of an ephah of fine flour. They shall be baked with yeast, for first fruits […]
echoes.note: The whole chapter unfolds on the Feast of Weeks/Pentecost (Lev 23:15-21, fifty days from Passover, with firstfruits offered), and the harvest of 'about three thousand souls' added (v.41) reads as the firstfruits of the eschatological harvest gathered on that very feast. Low verbal volume; calendrical and firstfruits-harvest coherence is the basis; contested as deliberate allusion.

echoes.text: Then those who feared Yahweh spoke one with another; and Yahweh listened, and heard, and a book of memory was written before him, for those who feared Yahweh, and who honored his name.
echoes.note: The devout, fearing community joined in fellowship and praise, growing daily, faintly recalls the remnant who 'feared the LORD and spoke with one another,' written in the book of remembrance. Very faint, thematic-coherence-only; contested.

places.name: Jerusalem
places.id: The City of David and Old City, on the spurs above the Kidron Valley, c. 50 km from the Mediterranean. Pre-Israelite Jebus; named here as the seat of Adoni-Zedek, leader of the southern coalition.

places.name: Nazareth
places.id: Modern en-Nasira / Nazareth in Lower Galilee, c. 30 km west of the Sea of Galilee. A village of perhaps 200-400 in the early first century, identified through continuous habitation, tomb evidence, and the third-century Caesarea inscription naming it as a priestly course settlement.

places.name: Judea
places.id: The Roman administrative province (later procuratorial province) covering the southern hill country of Israel — Jerusalem, the Judean wilderness, and territory south to the Negev. The Greco-Roman successor to the Hasmonean and Herodian Iudaea. Pin sits in the central hill country.

places.name: Parthia
places.id: The empire stretching from the Euphrates eastward across the Iranian plateau under the Arsacid dynasty (247 B.C. – A.D. 224). Rome's principal eastern rival in the apostolic period. Pin sits in the Parthian heartland near Hecatompylos / Damghan.

places.name: Media
places.id: The northwestern Iranian plateau, capital at Ecbatana (modern Hamadan). By the apostolic period a satrapy of the Parthian empire. The Medes appear as a distinct people in Acts 2 even though their kingdom had been absorbed centuries earlier.

places.name: Elam
places.id: The lowland region of southwestern Iran (Khuzestan), traditionally centered on Susa. By the first century the Hellenistic Susiana, governed under Parthian overlordship.

places.name: Mesopotamia
places.id: The land between the Tigris and Euphrates. In the apostolic period split between Roman client kingdoms in the upper basin (Edessa) and Parthian control of Babylonia. Pin sits in the middle Euphrates region.

places.name: Cappadocia
places.id: The interior Anatolian plateau, made a Roman province under Tiberius in A.D. 17. Famous in late antiquity for its volcanic-tuff landscape and rock-hewn churches; in the first century a primarily rural province with a mixed Hellenistic and Iranian-influenced elite.

places.name: Pontus
places.id: The Black Sea coast of northern Anatolia, the kingdom of Mithridates VI in the late Hellenistic period, partitioned into a Roman province and client states after 63 B.C. The home region of Aquila (Acts 18:2).

places.name: Asia
places.id: The Roman province (formed 129 B.C.) covering the western third of Anatolia, with Ephesus as its capital and the seven cities of Revelation 1-3 within its bounds. Distinct from 'Asia' as a continent and from the Seleucid use of the term for the wider Anatolian-Syrian sphere.

places.name: Phrygia
places.id: The west-central Anatolian plateau, a cultural region split administratively between Roman Asia (west) and Galatia (east) in the apostolic period. Pisidian Antioch and Iconium lay within the wider Phrygian zone.

places.name: Pamphylia
places.id: The narrow coastal plain of southern Anatolia between Lycia (west) and Cilicia (east), with Perga and Attalia as its principal cities. A Roman province (combined with Lycia under Vespasian).

places.name: Egypt
places.id: The Nile valley civilization, the land of Israel's bondage. Pin sits on the Nile near ancient Memphis.

places.name: Libya
places.id: The Roman province of Cyrenaica (later Libya superior), the coastal strip of north Africa west of Egypt. The phrase 'parts of Libya around Cyrene' in Acts 2:10 picks out the Pentapolis region around the city.

places.name: Cyrene
places.id: The chief Greek city of the Cyrenaican coast (modern Shahhat, Libya). A major Jewish community is attested in the apostolic period; Simon of Cyrene was conscripted to bear Jesus' cross (Mk 15:21).

places.name: Rome
places.id: The imperial capital. In Acts the city is the goal of Paul's career (1:8 'to the uttermost parts of the earth'; 19:21; 28:14-16) and the destination of his appeal to Caesar.

places.name: Crete
places.id: The largest of the Greek islands, a Roman province (combined with Cyrene) since 67 B.C. Paul's voyage to Rome touches the south coast at Fair Havens and Phoenix (Acts 27).

places.name: Arabia
places.id: In the New Testament principally the Nabataean kingdom east of the Jordan and the Dead Sea, with Petra as its capital — annexed as Roman Arabia in A.D. 106. Pin sits at Petra. Paul's 'three years in Arabia' of Gal 1:17 places him in this kingdom rather than the wider peninsula.

echoes.text: They made his grave with the wicked, and with a rich man in his death; although he had done no violence, neither was any deceit in his mouth.
echoes.note: "who did not sin, 'neither was deceit found in his mouth'" (2:22) quotes Isaiah 53:9 LXX, 'he did no lawlessness, nor was deceit (dolos) found in his mouth.' Verbatim citation of the Servant; anchors the Christ-as-suffering-Servant exemplum.

echoes.text: He was oppressed, yet when he was afflicted he didn’t open his mouth. As a lamb that is led to the slaughter, and as a sheep that before its shearers is mute, so he didn’t open his mouth.
echoes.note: "when he was cursed, didn't curse back. When he suffered, didn't threaten" (2:23) interprets Isaiah 53:7, 'he was afflicted yet opened not his mouth; like a lamb led to slaughter... he opens not his mouth.' The Servant's silent non-retaliation is the model for unjustly suffering servants.

echoes.text: Surely he has borne our sickness, and carried our suffering; yet we considered him plagued, struck by God, and afflicted.
echoes.note: "who his own self bore our sins in his body on the tree" (2:24) draws on Isaiah 53:4 LXX, 'he bears our sins (houtos tas hamartias hēmōn pherei),' fused with 53:12. The vicarious sin-bearing is the theological core of the Servant application.

echoes.text: Therefore will I divide him a portion with the great, and he shall divide the plunder with the strong; because he poured out his soul to death, and was numbered with the transgressors; yet he bore the sin of many, and made intercession for the transgressors.
echoes.note: "bore our sins in his body" (2:24) also reflects Isaiah 53:12, 'he bore the sins of many (autos hamartias pollōn anēnegken)' — the verb anapherō ('bore/bore up') matches 53:12 LXX, making this a distinct source-clause alongside 53:4.

echoes.text: But he was pierced for our transgressions. He was crushed for our iniquities. The punishment that brought our peace was on him; and by his wounds we are healed.
echoes.note: "by whose stripes you were healed" (2:24) is a near-verbatim citation of Isaiah 53:5 LXX, 'by his bruise (tō mōlōpi autou) we were healed.' Distinctive rare word mōlōps marks high volume.

echoes.text: All we like sheep have gone astray. Everyone has turned to his own way; and Yahweh has laid on him the iniquity of us all.
echoes.note: "For you were going astray like sheep; but now have returned" (2:25) reworks Isaiah 53:6 LXX, 'all we like sheep have gone astray (planēthēmen).' The verb 'gone astray' + 'sheep' is verbatim from the Servant song; the 'returned' supplies the gospel reversal.

echoes.text: For thus says the Lord Yahweh: Behold, I myself, even I, will search for my sheep, and will seek them out. As a shepherd seeks out his flock in the day that he is among his sheep that are scattered abroad, so will I seek out my sheep; and I will deliver them out of all places where they have been scattered in the cloudy and dark day. I will bring them out from the peoples, and gather them from the countries, and will bring them into their own land; and I […]
echoes.note: "returned to the Shepherd and Overseer of your souls" (2:25) draws on the divine-shepherd oracle of Ezekiel 34, where God himself seeks and gathers the scattered sheep; the straying-sheep/returning-to-shepherd movement of Isa 53:6 is completed with Ezekiel's restoring shepherd imagery.

echoes.text: After the suffering of his soul, he will see the light and be satisfied. My righteous servant will justify many by the knowledge of himself; and he will bear their iniquities.
echoes.note: "that we, having died to sins, might live to righteousness" (2:24) resonates with Isaiah 53:11, the Servant who 'makes many righteous (dikaiōsai dikaion)'; the righteousness outcome of sin-bearing parallels the Servant's justifying work.

echoes.text: Yahweh is my shepherd: I shall lack nothing.
echoes.note: "the Shepherd... of your souls" (2:25) faintly recalls the Lord-as-shepherd of Psalm 23:1; a thematic resonance of God's pastoral care behind the title applied to Christ.

echoes.text: He was despised, and rejected by men; a man of suffering, and acquainted with disease. He was despised as one from whom men hide their face; and we didn’t respect him.
echoes.note: The pattern of patient unjust suffering held up as example (2:19-21) reflects the despised-and-rejected Servant of Isaiah 53:3, conditioning the whole exemplum before the formal citations begin.

echoes.attribution: Catena, CC BY-SA 4.0 (Wilson Pruitt / Wroot Press)

echoes.text: Yahweh’s word came to me, saying, Son of man, prophesy against the shepherds of Israel, prophesy, and tell them, even to the shepherds, Thus says the Lord Yahweh: Woe to the shepherds of Israel who feed themselves! Shouldn’t the shepherds feed the sheep? You eat the fat, and you clothe yourself with the wool, you kill the fatlings; but you don’t feed the sheep. You haven’t strengthened the diseased, neither have you healed that which was sick, neither […]
echoes.note: Ezekiel 34 is the controlling subtext for the whole discourse: false shepherds who do not enter rightly and exploit the flock vs. the true shepherd. The thief/robber who climbs in 'some other way' answers Ezekiel's self-feeding shepherds, and the rightful shepherd entering by the door answers the LORD's own shepherding. High volume, recurrence across the chapter, and coherence with John's polemic against Israel's leaders.

echoes.text: “Let Yahweh, the God of the spirits of all flesh, appoint a man over the congregation, who may go out before them, and who may come in before them, and who may lead them out, and who may bring them in; that the congregation of Yahweh not be as sheep which have no shepherd.”
echoes.note: Moses asks the LORD to appoint a shepherd who leads Israel 'out' and brings them 'in,' so the congregation not be sheep without a shepherd. John's shepherd who 'leads them out' (v.3) and goes before them (v.4) echoes the leading-out/going-before language of the appointment of a shepherd over Israel.

echoes.text: for he is our God. We are the people of his pasture, and the sheep in his care. Today, oh that you would hear his voice!
echoes.note: 'The sheep listen to his voice' and refusal to follow strangers resonates with 'the sheep of his hand. Today, if you would hear his voice.' The motif of the flock recognizing and hearing the shepherd's voice is verbally and thematically coherent.

echoes.text: Thus says Yahweh my God: “Feed the flock of slaughter. Their buyers slaughter them, and go unpunished. Those who sell them say, ‘Blessed be Yahweh, for I am rich;’ and their own shepherds don’t pity them. For I will no more pity the inhabitants of the land,” says Yahweh; “but, behold, I will deliver the men everyone into his neighbor’s hand, and into the hand of his king. They will strike the land, and out of their hand I will not deliver them.” So I fed […]
echoes.note: Zechariah's flock 'doomed to slaughter' under worthless shepherds who do not care for the sheep, and the breaking of the bond with the flock, anticipates John's thieves/robbers contrasted with the true shepherd. Recurs more strongly at vv.11-13, but the false-shepherd indictment colors the parable here.

echoes.text: Know that Yahweh, he is God. It is he who has made us, and we are his. We are his people, and the sheep of his pasture.
echoes.note: 'We are his people, and the sheep of his pasture' supplies the flock-belonging frame behind the shepherd who knows his own and calls them by name. Faint; competes with Psalm 95 and the broader shepherd-of-Israel topos.

echoes.text: Yahweh’s word came to me, saying, Son of man, prophesy against the shepherds of Israel, prophesy, and tell them, even to the shepherds, Thus says the Lord Yahweh: Woe to the shepherds of Israel who feed themselves! Shouldn’t the shepherds feed the sheep? You eat the fat, and you clothe yourself with the wool, you kill the fatlings; but you don’t feed the sheep. You haven’t strengthened the diseased, neither have you healed that which was sick, neither […]
echoes.note: 'All who came before me are thieves and robbers' continues the indictment of Israel's bad shepherds in Ezekiel 34, while 'find pasture' (v.9) directly echoes the LORD's promise to feed his flock in good pasture (Ezek 34:14). Strong recurrence and coherence with the governing subtext.

echoes.text: This is the gate of Yahweh; the righteous will enter into it.
echoes.note: 'This is the gate of the LORD; the righteous will enter into it' undergirds Jesus' self-identification as the door through which one 'enters in' and 'will be saved.' Psalm 118 is a major Johannine/Synoptic source and the entering-and-being-saved language coheres with the entrance-gate motif.

echoes.text: Woe to the shepherds who destroy and scatter the sheep of my pasture! says Yahweh. Therefore thus says Yahweh, the God of Israel, against the shepherds who feed my people: You have scattered my flock, and driven them away, and have not visited them; behold, I will visit on you the evil of your doings, says Yahweh. I will gather the remnant of my flock out of all the countries where I have driven them, and will bring them again to their folds; and they […]
echoes.note: 'Woe to the shepherds who destroy and scatter the sheep' parallels the thief who 'comes to steal, kill, and destroy.' Jeremiah promises to set up shepherds who will feed the flock so none is lacking, coherent with John's life-giving shepherd over against destroyers.

echoes.text: who may go out before them, and who may come in before them, and who may lead them out, and who may bring them in; that the congregation of Yahweh not be as sheep which have no shepherd.”
echoes.note: 'Will go in and go out, and will find pasture' echoes the shepherd who leads Israel 'out' and brings them 'in' so they may be led to pasture. The go-in/go-out idiom for secure shepherded life is shared, though common in the OT.

registers.label: Spare
lines: The shepherd calls his own sheep by name.
We know his voice, and we follow.
He leads us to green pastures and still water.
He restores our souls.
Though we walk through the valley of shadow,
we will fear no evil, for he is with us.
Christ is risen!
Christ is risen, alleluia!

registers.label: Immersive
lines: Listen — the shepherd is calling, naming his own, and the gate stands open for everyone who knows his voice.
Christ is risen, alleluia!
He leads us down to green pastures and the quiet water, and there, beside it, he restores the tired soul.
Christ is risen, alleluia!
Even through the valley where the shadow falls, his rod and his staff are near, and we are not afraid.
Christ is risen, alleluia!
He spreads a table for us, and goodness and mercy follow us home all the days of our lives.
Christ is risen, alleluia!

registers.label: Hybrid
lines: The good shepherd calls us each by name.
Christ is risen, alleluia!
He leads us to still water and restores our souls.
Christ is risen, alleluia!
Through the valley of shadow we will not fear.
Christ is risen, alleluia!
He sets a table before us. Come, let us worship.
Christ is risen, alleluia!
